intro: This guide helps you lead thirteen weekly sessions on Corrie ten Boom (For Teens), the true story of a Dutch watchmaker’s daughter whose family hid Jewish people from the Nazis in their narrow house in Haarlem, who survived Ravensbrück concentration camp after her father and her sister Betsie died, and who spent the rest of her life telling the world that Jesus is Victor and that forgiveness is possible because God gives it. It is written for teens aged about 13 to 18, and works well for a youth group, a homeschool or a small group. The book is careful to separate what the records show from what grew in the retelling, which makes it a good place for teens to think about courage, conscience, suffering, thanksgiving and forgiveness.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10–15 minutes). Do the activity (about 10 minutes). Then close by praying the chapter’s prayer, or one of your own (2 minutes).

To prepare, read the chapter yourself beforehand and look over the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens. This is a Holocaust story, and from chapter 3 onward it includes persecution and murder of Jewish people, beatings, prison, humiliation and death in the camps, and the deaths of Corrie’s father and sister. The book tells it honestly without dwelling on horror, but some teens will feel it deeply, and some may carry their own grief or trauma, so give space, never ask anyone to share painful experiences in front of the group, and know who you would refer a young person to; the book itself points readers to a parent, pastor, teacher, doctor or crisis line. Speak of Jewish people with the respect the ten Booms showed them. When you reach the chapters on forgiveness, make clear that forgiving someone is not the same as excusing them, cancelling justice, or staying near someone who is still causing harm, and that no one should be pushed to forgive or contact a person who has hurt them.

weeks.summary: The ten Boom family runs a watch shop in a narrow house in Haarlem called the Beje, built on a century of honest, trusted work. Family tradition says Corrie’s grandfather Willem began a weekly prayer for the Jewish people and the peace of Jerusalem in 1844, and her father Casper called the Jews “God’s ancient people.” Corrie is born in Amsterdam in 1892 and grows up in a crowded house where there is always room for one more at the table. The big idea: courage in a crisis grows out of what we practise when nothing is at stake.

memory_verse.text: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem! “May they be secure who love you!”

activity.title: Practice Before Pressure
steps: Read the chapter’s line: “What you practise when nothing is at stake is what you will have when everything is.”
List together the ten Booms’ ordinary habits: weekly prayer, honest work, an open table.
In small groups, list three ordinary habits teens could build now that would prepare them to do the right thing under pressure.
Ask each person to choose one group of people in danger or pushed aside and write their name somewhere they will see it each morning to pray for them this week.

weeks.summary: Corrie’s mother, weakened by strokes, keeps loving through the little she can still do, and dies in 1921. Around then the young man Corrie hoped to marry chooses someone else, and her father tells her not to kill the love but to give it to God and let him send it elsewhere. Corrie never marries; she becomes a watchmaker, starts the Triangle clubs for girls, teaches the faith to people with intellectual disabilities and helps foster children. The big idea: when love has nowhere to go, God can redirect it, and faithfulness in small things prepares us for what we can’t yet see.

memory_verse.text: God settles the solitary in a home; he leads out the prisoners to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a parched land.

activity.title: Redirecting Love
steps: Read aloud Casper’s advice about love that has nowhere to go.
Ask everyone to write down privately one disappointment they are carrying, in one sentence, as a prayer to God.
As a group, brainstorm people in your community whom few others notice, as Corrie noticed people with disabilities.
Have each person choose one person from that list, or from their own life, and plan one kind thing to do for them this week.

weeks.summary: In May 1940 Germany invades the Netherlands, and step by step Dutch Jews are registered, banned, made to wear the yellow star and deported; about three in four are murdered. The elderly Casper wants to wear the star beside his Jewish neighbours, and Corrie’s turning point comes when she hears a Jewish doctor tucking in his children and realises the secret police could take them any night. The chapter is honest that most Dutch Christians kept their heads down, and compares the family to Esther, placed where she was “for such a time as this.” The big idea: evil grows by small injustices we accept in silence, and we are responsible for where God has put us.

memory_verse.text: For if you keep silent at this time, relief and deliverance will rise for the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?

activity.title: One Small Step at a Time
steps: Read out the list of restrictions placed on Dutch Jews in the chapter, one at a time.
After each one, ask the group how ordinary people might have explained to themselves why they said nothing.
Discuss: why does evil rarely ask for something monstrous all at once?
Ask everyone to think of one place, at school, online or at home, where someone is shut out or treated unfairly, and write down privately one small way to refuse to go along.

weeks.summary: Helping begins one knock at a time, as Jews who have been warned arrive at the Beje and the family searches for safer hiding places. By 1943 the house is a hub for around eighty resistance workers, and Corrie passes on smuggled ration cards hidden in a secret step. The chapter raises the question of lying: Corrie’s sister Nollie refused to lie and was arrested, while Corrie practised deception, and the chapter shows how Scripture and Christians have differed on it. The big idea: God rarely shows the whole road; he shows us the next person at the door.

memory_verse.text: Rescue those who are being taken away to death; hold back those who are stumbling to the slaughter.

activity.title: Nollie or Corrie?
steps: Explain that Nollie refused to lie even to protect someone, while Corrie believed the work required deception.
Divide the group into two sides, one for each sister’s view, and give them three minutes to find reasons from the chapter, including the midwives and Rahab.
Let each side present, then discuss what both sisters agreed on: “We must obey God rather than men.”
Finish by asking everyone to think of one person who needs help right now and one step they could take this week.

weeks.summary: A resistance architect known as Mr. Smit builds a hidden room behind a false wall in Corrie’s bedroom, and the family drills with buzzers and a stopwatch until everyone can hide in seventy seconds. Over the months more than eighty people pass through the house, including the cantor Eusie, Mary van Itallie and the student Hans Poley. Life in hiding is full of music, evening classes and laughter, yet the family never confuses the brick wall with God. The big idea: be practical about danger, but don’t let it have the last word, for God is our true hiding place.

memory_verse.text: You are a hiding place for me; you preserve me from trouble; you surround me with shouts of deliverance.

activity.title: Prepared and Joyful
steps: Talk about how the Beje both drilled for danger and kept music, classes and laughter going.
Ask everyone to write down privately one thing they have been avoiding: a conversation, a deadline, a plan.
Have them write three practical steps to prepare for it properly.
As a group, plan one simply joyful thing you could do together, and thank God for it on purpose.

weeks.summary: On 28 February 1944 the Beje is raided while six people hide behind the false wall. Corrie and Betsie are beaten, the family is arrested, and at the police station Willem reads Psalm 91 and Casper prays for the last time. The six in hiding are freed two days later by friendly police, but the chapter tells the truth that Mary van Itallie was later arrested and murdered at Auschwitz, while Eusie survived. The big idea: Psalm 91’s deepest promise is not that nothing bad will happen, but that God himself is our refuge in trouble.

memory_verse.text: He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say to the LORD, “My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust.”

activity.title: Reading Psalm 91 Honestly
steps: Read Psalm 91 aloud together, slowly.
Have everyone underline or note each promise that God will be with them, as opposed to promises that nothing will go wrong.
Discuss: what did it mean for the ten Booms to read this psalm on the night its protection seemed to fail?
Close by praying the psalm together for someone the group knows who is going through something hard.

weeks.summary: Corrie is taken to Scheveningen prison, where her father dies nine days after his arrest, still saying he would help the Jews again. Sick and in solitary confinement, she sings, feeds a line of ants and learns of his death from Nollie’s letter. Questioned by Lieutenant Rahms, she tells him God’s love reaches especially the weak and despised, and he confides his own darkness to her. The big idea: God didn’t take Corrie’s loneliness away; he came into it, and we don’t have to sit in darkness alone.

memory_verse.text: For my father and my mother have forsaken me, but the LORD will take me in.

activity.title: My People
steps: Read the chapter’s lines on Corrie finding God close in her lonely cell.
Discuss how loneliness and grief can play tricks on us, telling us nobody cares.
Ask everyone to write down privately the name of one person they could talk to honestly if things got dark.
Encourage them to let that person know this week that they are glad they are in their life, and remind the group who they can go to for help.

weeks.summary: Corrie and Betsie are reunited on a train and sent to Vught concentration camp, where a humiliating shower in front of soldiers is stopped before their turn, which Corrie counts as answered prayer. Betsie starts a society against grumbling, Corrie leads Sunday worship and a discussion group, and she admits honestly that she longed for home and held out only by God’s grace. After witnessing the execution of male prisoners, she learns to bring the world’s sorrows to God, and pictures life as the tangled back of a piece of embroidery. The big idea: God doesn’t promise we will avoid the waters and the fire, but that he will be with us in them.

memory_verse.text: When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you.

activity.title: Betsie’s Society
steps: Read out Betsie’s three rules: don’t grumble, don’t speak ill of anyone, speak encouragingly to others.
Ask the group to predict which rule they would find hardest and why.
Have everyone make a simple tally chart for the week to note privately when they slip.
Commit together to try Betsie’s society for seven days, and agree to talk next week about how it went, without sharing details.

weeks.summary: At Ravensbrück the sisters smuggle in a small Bible and hold Bible readings for crowds of women of many nations in the lice-ridden Barracks 28. The chapter compares the famous fleas story with Corrie’s earlier account and notes that Paul says to give thanks in everything, not for everything. Corrie shares drops from a vitamin bottle that by her account lasted far longer than it should have, and she warns of the selfishness she calls “the Ravensbrück that destroys.” The big idea: thanksgiving in every circumstance and giving to others first can survive even in the darkest place.

memory_verse.text: Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you.

activity.title: In, Not For
steps: Discuss the chapter’s difference between giving thanks in everything and giving thanks for everything.
Ask everyone to write down privately three things they can honestly thank God for, including one from inside a hard part of their week.
As a group, list ways the attitude of “every woman for herself” shows up in teen life.
Challenge everyone to give away something they’d rather keep this week: time, attention or money.

weeks.summary: Betsie, always the weaker in body, becomes the stronger in faith, pitying those who hurt her and sheltering Corrie from despair, while Corrie cares for her in practical ways. The sisters plan to open homes after the war and travel to tell what God has done. Betsie grows sick and dies on 16 December 1944, calling after Corrie, “Remember now, both of us,” and after desolation Corrie finds peace and gives Betsie’s place to a Russian woman nobody would take in. The big idea: there is no depth, not even death, where God is not already there.

memory_verse.text: If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there!

activity.title: Hiding Places for Each Other
steps: Read the line from Corrie’s 1945 book that she was like Betsie’s hiding place, and talk about how the sisters sheltered each other.
Ask everyone to think of the person who has most been a hiding place for them.
Have them write a short note to that person naming one specific way they have sheltered them, to give or send this week.
Remind the group gently who they can talk to if grief feels too heavy.

weeks.summary: After Betsie’s death, Corrie falls ill after a punishing roll-call and is then unexpectedly called for discharge, spending a terrible week in the hospital barracks where she helps the dying and leads a young woman named Oelie to faith. She believes God freed her eight hours before the bitter cold, and reaches home in January 1945 to find her piano and her father’s chair. The chapter checks the later story of a clerical error and finds no record of it, while affirming the danger was real. The big idea: like a bird escaped from a snare, we may not know how God rescued us, only that we are free.

memory_verse.text: We have escaped like a bird from the snare of the fowlers; the snare is broken, and we have escaped!

activity.title: Rescue Stories
steps: Ask everyone to think of a time they were rescued from something, big or small, even if they don’t know how it happened.
Have each person write a few lines about it for themselves.
Invite a few volunteers who are comfortable to tell their story in a sentence or two.
Discuss why the chapter bothers to check the clerical error story, and why telling the truth carefully matters.

weeks.summary: In freed Holland Corrie refuses to join crowds humiliating women accused of relationships with German soldiers. Her family has lost Casper, Betsie, Willem’s son Kik and later Willem himself, and the chapter is careful about what is and isn’t known of the informer. On 19 June 1945 she writes to the man she believed betrayed them, naming exactly what it cost and forgiving him, then opens homes for people recovering from the war, including former collaborators and refugees. The big idea: forgiveness is an act of the will that doesn’t wait for feelings, and it isn’t pretending or cancelling justice.

memory_verse.text: But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.

activity.title: What Forgiveness Is and Isn’t
steps: Draw two columns, “Forgiveness is” and “Forgiveness isn’t,” and fill them in together from the chapter.
Make sure the “isn’t” column includes pretending nothing happened, cancelling justice and staying close to someone who is still causing harm.
Ask everyone to think privately of one smaller hurt they need to forgive, and write for themselves what it cost and that they choose to forgive.
Remind the group that they do not need to send anything, and that for serious hurts they should talk with a trusted adult first.

weeks.summary: Corrie tells of meeting a former Ravensbrück guard in Munich in 1947 who asks for her forgiveness; unable to feel it, she prays for Jesus’ love and holds out her hand, and feels warmth flow through her. The chapter notes this rests on her own memory, and that she found she had to keep forgiving, even friends in small things. She travels to more than sixty countries with the message “Jesus is Victor,” is honoured by Yad Vashem, and dies on her ninety-first birthday in 1983. The big idea: God’s love has been poured into our hearts, so we can hold out our hand before the feelings arrive.

memory_verse.text: Hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

activity.title: Two Hiding Places
steps: Look back over the thirteen weeks and list together the ways the brick hiding place saved lives and the ways it couldn’t.
Then list the ways Corrie found God to be her hiding place when the wall could no longer protect her.
Read aloud the prayer from the chapter: “Jesus, I can’t forgive them on my own. Give me your love for them.”
Give everyone a quiet minute to pray it privately about someone they find hard to forgive, and to write for themselves one small step of obedience.
